pages.text: Ivy said, “Every mystery has clues. The mystery is: why does our road flood every time it rains? The clues are in the drains.” She drew a badge that said Drain Detectives. Musah drew a magnifying glass on it. Maa Abla read the badge and nodded. “Detectives must follow three rules,” she said. “Stay safe, be honest, and be kind.”
sentences: Ivy said, “Every mystery has clues.
The mystery is: why does our road flood every time it rains?
The clues are in the drains.” She drew a badge that said Drain Detectives.
Musah drew a magnifying glass on it.
Maa Abla read the badge and nodded.
“Detectives must follow three rules,” she said.
“Stay safe, be honest, and be kind.”
pages.alt: Children in yellow vests hold a hand-drawn badge reading Drain Detectives beside their teacher.

pages.text: The first rule was the most important. “Nobody goes into a drain or leans over an open one,” said Maa Abla. “You look from the pavement, with an adult beside you. You wear shoes. You wash your hands afterwards.” The detectives agreed. Ivy wrote the rule at the top of the page and underlined it three times.

pages.alt: A teacher points to a safety poster showing children standing on the pavement and not touching an open drain.

pages.text: The detectives walked the road from the school gate to the main junction. They counted twenty drains. They marked each one on a map: clear, half-blocked or blocked. Musah took a photo of each blocked one, with the date. Ivy noted what was in it: sachets, bottles, mud, leaves, a broken bucket and, in one place, building sand.

Ivy noted what was in it: sachets, bottles, mud, leaves, a broken bucket and, in one place, building sand.
pages.alt: Children with clipboards mark colours on a street map while one photographs a blocked drain from the pavement.

pages.text: Back at school, they counted the clues. Of the twenty drains, seven were clear, six were half-blocked and seven were blocked. “That is thirty-five per cent blocked,” said Ivy. “And six more are on the way,” said Musah. They made a bar chart in three colours. Maa Abla looked at it for a long time. “This is real evidence,” she said.

pages.alt: A bar chart with three coloured bars and a headline: 7 clear, 6 half-blocked, 7 blocked.

pages.text: The detectives found more clues. Three of the worst drains were near a stall where people washed cloth and threw the water and soap packets into the gutter. Two were near a building site where sand had washed in. One was blocked by a drainpipe that had been pushed in too far. “Different causes need different answers,” said Ivy. “Not just shouting at people.”

pages.alt: A drawing of three causes: a stall, a building site and a broken pipe, each marked on the map.

pages.text: First, they spoke to people kindly. They gave the stallholder a bin and showed her the chart. She laughed and said, “Nobody ever showed me. I thought the gutter was where water goes.” Then they wrote to the Assembly Member with their map, photos and chart. They did not insult anyone. They asked for three things: clear the seven blocked drains, cover the open one by the school gate and talk to the building site about the sand.

pages.text: Nothing happened for three weeks. Musah wanted to give up. “They never listen,” he said. Ivy shook her head. “Then we write again, and we invite them to see for themselves,” she said. They sent a second letter and put their map on the school gate. In the fourth week, workers arrived and cleared five drains. Then they stopped. “Five out of seven,” said Ivy. “It is a start. We are still counting.”

“Five out of seven,” said Ivy.

We are still counting.”
pages.alt: Workers clearing drains with shovels while children watch from the pavement and hold a counting board.

pages.text: The Drain Detectives did not fix everything. But the road flooded less, the stallholder used her bin, and the headteacher asked them to train the next class. Ivy added a line to the badge: Ask. Count. Share. Follow up. “Leaders are not enemies,” she told the new detectives. “They are people we need to help do their jobs. Evidence makes it easier.” The end.
